extracted.intended_audience: college composition instructors, journalism educators, and researchers in writing instruction
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of the effect of including basic news writing instruction in English Composition I on student outcomes (anxiety, self-assessment, attitudes, motivation, perceived practicality, grammar/mechanics, and writing skill). Study uses pre/post tests, questionnaires, a standardized grammar test, and holistic scoring of writing exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anxiety toward writing (Geer Fear Survey)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' anxiety about writing measured via items from the Geer Fear Survey (educationally-induced stimuli: 'failing a test,' 'writing papers for a grade,' 'teachers,' 'English classes,' 'spelling words,' 'reading'). In this study three items were grouped: 'writing papers for a grade,' 'English classes,' and 'spelling words.' Responses on a 0 (no reaction) to 6 (terror) scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the main hypothesis measure: pre- and post-semester administration; group means compared with t-tests (significance evaluated at .05). The study grouped/totaled responses for each student on the three items to compute grand means; change over a 17-week semester was analyzed. Note that the survey can be altered to add educational stimuli (as Raisman did).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-assessment of writing ability (questionnaire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' self-rating of their own writing ability measured by seven questionnaire items designed for the study, with responses on a 5 (usually 'excellent' or 'very') to 1 ('poor' or 'not at all') Likert scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre- and post-test administrations (Questionnaires A and B). Changes in rating distribution analyzed using chi-square tests (frequency of rating changes per item). No individual item showed a significant relationship with the treatment in this study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude toward writing (questionnaire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' attitudes about writing assessed via three questionnaire items (same Likert scale as above) designed to measure attitude toward writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre/post measurement; analyzed via chi-square on frequency distributions of rating changes. In this study none of the attitude items indicated a significant relationship with the news-writing treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to improve writing (questionnaire)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' motivation to learn and improve writing measured by four items on the study's questionnaire, using a 5-to-1 Likert scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured pre- and post-semester; distributional changes tested with chi-square. No significant treatment effect found in this study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived practicality of writing instruction for work after college
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' view of how practical/helpful the English Composition I instruction would be for the world of work, measured by three items on Questionnaire B (key item: 'How helpful for the world of work do you view the writing instruction you received in English Composition I this fall?'). Responses on a 5 (very) to 1 (not at all) scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyzed with chi-square; in this study the key item produced a statistically significant relationship with the news-writing treatment (Chi-square = 13.197, p = 0.010), indicating the treatment group viewed instruction as more practical for work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar and mechanics improvement (English 3200 test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress in grammar and mechanics measured by scores on the English 3200 pre-test and post-test (a programmed and usage textbook test by Joseph Blumenthal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change in scores compared between treatment and control groups using t-tests. In this study mean improvement for control = 4.46 points, treatment = 5.33 points; difference not statistically significant (p = 0.7363).

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing skills improvement (holistic writing exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvement in general writing skill measured by a writing assignment administered pre- and post-study, scored holistically by two instructors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two raters graded essays holistically; rater correlation reported as .84. The average of the two raters' scores was used; pre-test average subtracted from post-test to compute improvement. Groups compared using t-tests (in this study, control improvement = 0.5263, treatment = 0.7500; p = 0.3296, not significant).

rubrics_metrics.name: News-writing instructional features (operational definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: News writing content defined for the treatment: instruction in the basic form and style of news writing including the inverted pyramid, lead writing, short paragraphs, attribution to source material, use of third person, and an emphasis on conciseness and brevity; placed less emphasis on personal experience (subjective) writing and creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the concrete stylistic and structural features taught in the treatment half-semester; they contrast with traditional personal/expressive composition. The author suggests these features foster clarity, realistic audience awareness, and writing from a body of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional composition content (operational definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional content defined as the content of McCrimmon's Writing With A Purpose: instruction typically focuses on the five-paragraph essay (introduction, three body paragraphs with topic sentences, conclusion), expressive/personal writing, ornate vocabulary, and complex sentence structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the control condition for comparison with news-writing instruction. The study asserts that traditional instruction often emphasizes product over process and may not prepare students for workplace writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of instruction as a pedagogical criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle that composition instruction should expose students to a full range of compositional possibilities (multiple forms and styles), rather than privileging a single 'correct' form of discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounded in cited authorities (Weathers, Perelman, Kinneavy). Justified as a response to weak student skills, poor attitudes toward English, and lack of perceived practicality. Implies interdisciplinary approaches and inclusion of genres like news writing, technical and business writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of a realistic audience as an instructional quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion that instruction is more effective when students write for a realistic/meaningful audience (e.g., analogous to a publications office), which refines higher-order writing skills and increases student engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argued as an advantage of news/journalism instruction (students see immediate audience and consequences). Teachers should create tasks with real or simulated audiences to improve writing outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of '5 Ws and H' as a pre-writing technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of the journalistic '5 Ws and H' (who, what, when, where, why, how) to help students formulate questions for sources and content for stories; used as a pre-writing strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a common journalistic method that can be integrated into composition instruction to structure inquiry and content generation; useful beyond pure news pieces as a prewriting scaffold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on writing clarity, conciseness, and directness
rubrics_metrics.description: An evaluative standard that good journalistic writing is clear, simple, concise, and direct; contrasted with some English instruction that favors ornate or wordy prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by citations (Mencher, Williams, Hake & Williams). Teachers and graders should value clarity over unnecessary complexity; the literature suggests graders sometimes (problematically) prefer wordy prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement and statistical analysis practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended/used analytic procedures: use of descriptive statistics (frequencies, percentages, means), chi-square for categorical/Likert rating-change analyses, t-tests for comparing mean change scores on interval measures (Geer Fear Survey totals, English 3200 differences, holistic writing-score differences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report rater reliability (rater correlation .84) when using holistic scoring. Compare pre/post within and across groups; evaluate significance at conventional levels (e.g., p < .05). Acknowledge limitations of short-term measurement periods and recommend longitudinal designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional dosage and study design considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount/timing of news-writing instruction (in this study: one-half semester of news writing followed by eight weeks of traditional instruction) and random assignment of students to treatment and control groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design details (random assignment to one treatment and three control sections, pre/post testing) are crucial for valid comparisons. The author notes that limited dosage/time (one semester) may mask effects and recommends longer or longitudinal studies to detect slower-growing writing improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic grading as an evaluative method
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a holistic grading scale to evaluate essay/writing exercise responses, with multiple raters and reporting of interrater correlation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two raters used in the study; rater correlation reported (.84). Holistic scoring yields a single overall score per essay; average raters' scores for analysis. Ensure rater training and reliability checks.
